talks.title: Social Engineering for Covert Access Assignments | Dorota Kozlowska
talks.teaser: Examines social Engineering for Covert Access Assignments | Dorota Kozlowska and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
Overview: Dorota Kozlowska presents at Wild West Hackin' Fest Deadwood on social engineering techniques for covert access assignments, covering rapport-building and elicitation methods.

Key Topics: Social engineering as manipulation without technical exploitation; business email compromise case studies; ransomware via phishing; building positive rapport; and elicitation techniques for information gathering.

Technical Details: Kozlowska walks through Barbara Corcoran's BEC loss via lookalike email spoofing and the Cabarrus County 2018 ransomware incident via phishing, then teaches rapport-building through shared interests and open-source intelligence on targets.

Takeaways: Covert access assignments rely on human manipulation skills, not just technical exploitation. Practitioners must master rapport, elicitation, and pretext development while maintaining ethical boundaries.

talks.title: Jargon & Jigsaw: Shellcode Obfuscation | Mike Saunders
talks.teaser: Analyzes jargon & Jigsaw: Shellcode Obfuscation | Mike Saunders and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
Entropy and EDR Detection

Mike Saunders of Red Siege explains shellcode obfuscation through information-theory entropy. High-entropy payloads resist compression and often trigger EDR heuristics; encrypted shellcode therefore looks suspicious even when hidden inside loaders.

The Jargon Technique

His Jargon tool encodes shellcode as sequences of English words drawn from a large dictionary, dramatically lowering measured entropy. In demos, an AES-encrypted loader (~362 KB) barely compresses, while the same loader with an embedded word array balloons to ~15 MB yet compresses the dictionary by ~65%—signaling low randomness to static analysis.

Design Rationale

Saunders coined "jargon" deliberately: specialized vocabulary that obscures meaning from outsiders, analogous to how word-encoded shellcode confuses defensive tools. He notes parallel ideas (including emoji-encoded shellcode presented elsewhere) but positions Jargon as published open tooling.

Jigsaw and Takeaways

The talk also covers companion Jigsaw obfuscation approaches. Saunders urges defenders to understand that compressibility and entropy metrics can be gamed, and that creative encodings may bypass simplistic high-entropy detection without relying on traditional encryption alone.

talks.title: OSINT Gone Wild: How I Found Drug Traffickers and NarcoTerrorists Online | Schuyler Davis
talks.teaser: Examines OSINT Gone Wild: how teams Found Drug Traffickers and NarcoTerrorists Online | Schuyler Davis and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
Narco-Terrorism and Online Trafficking

OSINT analyst Schuyler Davis explains narco-terrorism—using kidnappings, assassinations, and bombings to deter law enforcement—and links it to U.S. gang activity beyond traditional cartels. Traffickers increasingly use Telegram for encrypted drug sales, menu-style ordering, and anti-screenshot features.

OSINT Toolkit and Tradecraft

Davis uses publicly available sources plus tools like PimEyes facial recognition, FaceCheck, and passive reconnaissance. He stresses sock-puppet accounts after accidentally liking a target page from a personal profile, and documents fentanyl's lethal potency amid a national overdose crisis.

Case Study One: Twitter to Arrest Records

Searching intentional keywords such as "join Telegram pills" surfaced dealers advertising counterfeit pills. One suspect posted self-photos alongside shipment images; FaceCheck matched a 2022 arrest for marijuana and unlawful weapon carry, yet the same account resumed selling drugs and illicit gun-conversion switches years later.

Case Study Two: Organized Network

A shared Telegram invite appeared across multiple Twitter promoters selling guns and drugs. When one hid their face behind cash, another affiliate exposed theirs, enabling identification of gang members—including youth recruited into a pink-themed crew—through arrest articles and Facebook linkage. Davis partners with law enforcement while teaching kindergarten CS.

talks.title: Solving Dumb Hacker Problems With Nix | Ryan Basden
talks.teaser: Details solving Dumb Hacker Problems With Nix | Ryan Basden and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
Hacker environment chaos

Ryan Basden, ex-Fox red team and pentest director, describes recurring "dumb hacker problems": broken dependencies, inconsistent tool versions, and ad-hoc VM sprawl. He turned to Nix after Arch Linux dotfiles failed to deliver the declarative reproducibility he expected.

What Nix actually is

Nix is simultaneously a package manager (drop-in for apt, brew, pacman), a pure functional expression language, and the foundation for NixOS declarative system configuration. Packages live in the Nix store with content-addressed paths, enabling rollbacks and identical environments across machines.

Practical hacker workflows

Basden covers home-manager dotfiles, ephemeral root filesystems that wipe on reboot while persisting the store, atomic generation rollbacks after breaking a desktop, and systemd-nspawn containers without Docker. Trade-offs include abstraction complexity and friction when Nix wraps systemd behaviors he prefers to manage directly.
